rows.original: Building Safety Coordinator · Kestrel Bay
What the ground actually did, and which instrument is entitled to say so.
Whether a building is safe to enter, and what that placard is worth.
The ground under the town, and why it behaved in two different ways.
What the concrete, the brick and the steel can still carry.
What might still happen, expressed as a number somebody can act on.
Cordons, notices and the cost of keeping people out of their own houses.
Structural engineer, Building Safety Coordinator's deputy

Nineteen years assessing buildings, six of them after earthquakes in three countries. She places a building on what the evidence supports and not one step further, and she has been overruled enough times to know exactly what it costs when she is right.

Her rule, said aloud most mornings: a placard is a claim about a building, and a claim you cannot trace is a guess wearing a colour.
Why does Okonkwo refuse to upgrade a placard on a walk-past?
A rapid assessment samples what is visible from outside
Rapid assessments are only valid for the first twenty-four hours after an event
A placard cannot legally be changed once it has been fixed to the door
Damage always shows on the outside of a building before the inside
Emergency manager for the district

Ran the response to two floods and a gas main before this. He thinks in what the town cannot do without: a hospital with nobody in it, a school that stays shut for a term, a port that stops paying wages. He is not careless and he is not in a hurry for its own sake.

His argument with Okonkwo is the fortnight's argument, and each of them is right on a day the other is wrong.
What does Halvorsen mean when he says an empty hospital has a cost?
Care not given elsewhere is also harm, and it does not appear on any inspection form
Empty buildings deteriorate faster than occupied ones do
The hospital loses its funding if it is closed for more than a week
An empty building cannot be inspected properly while the power is off
Geotechnical engineer

She wrote her thesis on the fill under this town, which nobody read at the time and four people have asked her for this week. She can tell you which streets were creek in 1910 and it turns out those are the streets with sand in them now.

She is the one who keeps saying that the buildings are not the story, the ground is.
Why does Navarro care which streets were a creek a century ago?
Loose saturated fill in an old channel is where liquefaction shows up
Old creek beds are where the water mains were laid and they break first
Historical maps are the only record of where the fault runs
Buildings on former creek beds are always older and therefore weaker
Materials engineer, testing laboratory

He breaks things for a living and is unromantic about it. Cores from a damaged column, coupons cut from a brace, a rebound hammer for the cases where nobody will let him cut anything: he wants a number with a method attached and treats everything else as an opinion.

He is patient with people and impatient with round figures nobody can source.
Why will Ferreira not accept a rebound hammer reading as a strength?
It measures surface hardness, which is a proxy that has to be calibrated against cores
The hammer only works on concrete poured within the last five years
Rebound readings are affected by the weather and are useless in the rain
A hammer test damages the surface and cannot be repeated
Seismologist, hazard and forecasting

Fits aftershock sequences for a living and spends most of the week explaining that a forecast is a rate and not a promise. She is careful in public and blunt in the room.

She keeps a printed copy of the sequence taped to the wall, updated by hand, because she says people believe a curve they watched being drawn.
What does Tanaka's aftershock forecast actually state?
A rate of events per day, with a range around it
The date on which the sequence will end
The magnitude of the next aftershock
Which fault segment will move next
Public information officer

She has to turn everything this office decides into something a person standing in the street can act on, in two sentences, without frightening anybody into doing something worse. She is the only one who reads the notices aloud before they go out.

Her test for a notice: what does somebody do differently after reading it?
What is Adeyemi's test for a public notice?
Whether somebody reading it does something different afterwards
Whether it uses only words in common use
Whether it has been approved by every agency involved
Whether it can be printed on a single side of paper
Network technician, Seismic Network

She maintains the vault on the bench above town and the four field stations below it, which means she is the only person who knows that two of them have been running on a clock that drifted since spring.

She is not embarrassed about it. She is the one who found it.
Why does Cardoso check the vault instrument against a second one?
A single instrument cannot show its own drift
Vault instruments are less accurate than field stations
Two instruments together record a wider frequency range
The vault instrument is only used for large events
Assessment engineer, second team

Came up from the city with the second wave of assessors and has placarded more buildings this week than most engineers do in a career. He is fast, and he knows the risk in being fast, which is why he writes down what he did not look at.

The list of what he did not look at is the most useful document in the office.
Why does Whitcombe keep a second list beside his placards?
A placard says nothing about the parts of a building nobody could get to
A second list is required by the standard before a placard can be changed later
It records which buildings he expects to collapse in an aftershock
Inspectors are rotated, so the next one needs to know who was there
Geotechnical field technician

Logs the ground: cone tests where a rig can get in, hand augers where it cannot, and a photograph of every sand fan in the Flats with a scale bar in it.

The photographs are turning into the best record anybody has of what the ground did.
Why does Mbeki put a scale bar in every photograph?
Without it the picture records that ejecta happened, not how much
Photographs taken without a scale bar cannot be entered as evidence at an inquiry
The bar keeps the camera at a fixed distance from the ground
It marks which photographs were taken after the first aftershock
Laboratory technician, Materials & Testing

Runs the press. Cuts, caps and crushes cores, and keeps the chain of custody that makes the result mean anything — which building, which column, which face, which day.

She has refused two samples this week for arriving without a label.
Why does Sørensen refuse an unlabelled core?
A strength belongs to one column in one building, and an unlabelled core belongs to none
Unlabelled cores dry out on the bench before the press is free to test them
The press cannot be calibrated without knowing the concrete's age
Regulations require every sample to carry the name of the engineer who cut it
Hospital facilities manager

He has ninety beds, a yellow placard on his front door and no idea when either of those changes. He knows his building better than anybody assessing it, and he knows that is not the same as being able to say it is safe.

He is not fighting the process. He is asking it to hurry, precisely.
Why can Ives not simply declare his own building safe?
Knowing a building well is not the same as having assessed what the earthquake did to it
Facilities managers are not permitted to enter a building that carries a yellow placard
He has no access to the design drawings for the upper floors
A declaration by the occupier would invalidate the insurance
Ward councillor for the Flats

Represents the half of town that got the worse earthquake and has the smaller houses. She turns up to every meeting with a list of who is sleeping where, and she can name the streets that have been cordoned longest.

She is not against the cordons. She wants somebody to say when they end.
What is Delacroix actually asking the office for?
The condition each stretch of cordon would have to meet to come down
A guaranteed date on which every street reopens
Compensation for every household still unable to get back into its own house
A second opinion from an engineer she chooses herself
The notice fixed to a building after an inspection — green to enter, yellow for restricted use, red for no entry.
The point on the surface directly above where the fault started to slip.
A single number for the size of an earthquake, on a scale where each unit is about thirty-two times the energy.
How strongly the ground shook at one particular place, which differs across a town in one earthquake.
Wet, loosely packed ground losing its strength while it is shaken, and behaving like a heavy liquid.
Sand and water that reached the surface from below, left as grey fans in the street.
Ground that was placed by people rather than laid down by nature, often dredged and pumped into position.
Solid rock beneath the ground surface, which shakes only lightly where loose fill shakes hard.
Soft ground magnifying shaking, so two places the same distance from an earthquake feel different ones.
The time a building takes to sway back and forth once when it is pushed and let go.
What happens when the ground shakes at close to a building's own natural period, so each push adds to the last.
The total horizontal force an earthquake applies at the bottom of a building.
The route a force takes down through a building to the ground; if it stops anywhere, that is where the damage goes.
A floor with much lower stiffness than the storeys above it, usually an open ground floor, which takes all the movement.
A material's ability to bend a long way without breaking, which is what lets a building absorb an earthquake.
Brick or stone with no steel in it, strong when pressed and weak when pulled sideways.
What a part can carry, divided by what was required of it.
A smaller earthquake following the main one, on the same fault system, becoming rarer as time passes.
A boundary keeping people out of an area, and a decision with a cost on both sides of it.
A break in the rock where the two sides have moved past each other, and can move again.
Water pressure in the gaps inside the ground, which holds the packed particles apart.
Ground that is not tightly packed, so shaking can settle it into a smaller space.
Ground in which every gap is already full of water.
How much weight the ground can take before it fails under a building.
A force that slides one part of a wall or column past the part beside it.
How much a part of a building can carry before it fails.
How much the earthquake actually required that part to carry.
Two towns, one earthquake
Work out why the same shaking wrecked one half of Kestrel Bay and spared the other.
Upper Town lost its chimneys. The Flats lost its streets. Both are the same distance from the source.

Friday, three days after, and the first thing anybody says on walking into the base is that it makes no sense. Upper Town, on the granite bench, has parapets in the street and almost every building standing. The Flats, eleven hundred metres away on the same side of the same fault, have sand in the gutters, a six-storey block leaning at eight degrees and a wharf that moved two metres. Marisol Okonkwo will not sign an assessment programme until she can say why. Elena Navarro thinks she already knows and wants a borehole to prove it. Today you read the two records side by side, work out what the ground did to the shaking on its way up, and decide which half of town gets the assessors first.
One earthquake produces as many shakings as there are grounds to shake, and the ground is the difference.
The same event, recorded twice
Compare the two records from one earthquake
Seismic Network

Inês Cardoso has the vault record from the bench and the field station record from Bay Road. Same event, same minute, eleven hundred metres apart. One trace is short and sharp, the other is three times taller and goes on for half a minute longer.
A record describes one place, so two records of one earthquake can disagree and both be right.
an instrument records the shaking where it stands, not the earthquake itself
What does the difference between the two records mean?

Waves slow down as they come up into softer ground, and slow waves carry the same energy with bigger motions, so the shaking grows. Soft ground also rings: it holds the motion and gives it back over several more seconds, at the periods the layer itself prefers. Rock does neither. That is why the two records differ by a factor of three at eleven hundred metres, and it is the reason the same earthquake destroyed one half of this town and rattled the other.
One of the two instruments is faulty and its record should be discarded.
The soft ground under the Flats amplified and lengthened the shaking.
The Flats are closer to the epicentre, which is why the shaking there was stronger.
The Flats record includes aftershocks that the vault instrument was not running for.
Both instruments checked out against a second sensor this morning; the difference is real.
Eleven hundred metres is nothing against a source twenty kilometres away, so distance cannot explain a factor of three.
Both records cover the same ninety seconds, and the aftershocks are on separate traces.
Ground that people put there
Say what the ground under the Flats is made of
Geotechnical
Navarro has an 1892 survey and a photograph from 1948. Where Bay Road now runs there was a tidal creek, and the port was pumped into place out of the dredger over four summers.
Hydraulic fill is loose, saturated and young, which is the recipe for liquefaction.
ground can be natural or placed by people

Fill pumped from a dredger settles loose and stays loose: the grains are dropped through water rather than pressed together over centuries, and the water never leaves. Loose, saturated and uniform is precisely the ground that liquefies, because shaking can push the grains closer and the water has nowhere to go. Rock is none of those things. The old creek line matters because it is where the loosest and wettest material sits, and it is where every sand fan in this town came out.
Loose and saturated, so shaking can pack it and the water pressure rises.
Stiff and drained, so it passes the shaking on almost unchanged.
The loosest and wettest of all, which is where the sand fans appeared.
Consolidated by its own weight over time, which is why age is a defence.
Hydraulic fill is dropped through water, so it settles loose and stays saturated.
The granite bench is neither loose nor saturated, so its behaviour under shaking is nothing like the fill.
The old creek line is where the loosest wettest material sits, which is why the fans follow it.
Age matters because ground gains strength as it consolidates, and eighty years is young.
Hydraulic fill, pumped in from a dredger in the 1940s.
The granite bench under Upper Town.
The line of the 1892 tidal creek.
Ground that has been in place for ten thousand years.
Where the first day of assessment goes
Send the assessors somewhere first
Structural Assessment
Six assessors, two halves of a town and one day. Okonkwo wants them where the buildings are worst. Bram Halvorsen wants them where the most people are waiting to go home.
Send inspectors where the answer will change what happens next, not where the damage photographs best.
an assessment programme is a queue, and the order is a decision
Where does the first day of assessment go?

An inspection is worth what it changes. Four hundred households are sleeping in a hall waiting on a placard, and most of those buildings will come back green or yellow, so a day spent there sends hundreds of people home. Marina Court is already cordoned and already empty, so an assessment today changes nobody's night. The Parade is the same: the damage has happened, the street is shut, and knowing more about it this afternoon moves nothing. Damage is not the same as urgency.
The Flats terraces — 400 households out, most repairable.
Marina Court, which is visibly leaning and already cordoned with nobody inside.
Upper Town's timber houses, which are off their piles but standing.
The Parade, where the parapets already fell and the street is closed.
Marina Court is cordoned and empty, so a placard on it today changes nobody's night.
The timber houses are standing and their occupants are mostly back in already.
The Parade's street is closed and its damage is done; more detail there moves nothing today.
The number everybody has already heard
Pin the magnitude and the location down, and separate them from what people felt.
Two agencies published two magnitudes, and the difference is being read as a disagreement.

Saturday, and the town has two numbers for the same earthquake. One agency said 6.6 within twenty minutes; another said 6.8 six hours later. Rei Tanaka can explain the difference in one sentence to an engineer and has spent the morning failing to explain it to a radio station. Funmi Adeyemi has to put something in a notice by four. Meanwhile Inês Cardoso has found that two field stations have been running on a clock that drifted since spring, which changes where the epicentre plots. Today you locate the earthquake properly, say what its magnitude is and what it is not, and write down what the difference between 6.6 and 6.8 actually means.
A magnitude is a measurement with a method attached, and revising it is the method working.
How far away it started
Locate the source from arrival times
Seismic Network
The vault trace shows the P arrival at 04:12:19 and the S arrival at 04:12:32. Cardoso wants the distance before anybody draws a circle on a map.
The gap between the two arrivals grows with distance, so one station gives a distance and three give a place.
P waves travel faster than S waves through the same rock
Estimate the distance from this station to the source.

Both waves leave at the same instant and travel the same path, but the P wave is faster, so the gap between their arrivals is a clock that has been running since the earthquake started. For shallow crust the two speeds work out at roughly eight kilometres for every second of gap. One station turns that into a radius and knows only that the source is somewhere on a circle; three stations turn three circles into a point, which is why a network exists at all.
About 100 km.
The P wave arrived at 04:12:19 and the S wave at 04:12:32. Use 8 km for each second of separation.
Choose the two arrival times and the constant.

About a hundred kilometres to the source. The magnitude and the depth are both real numbers about this earthquake and neither belongs in this calculation — one is how big it was, the other is how deep, and this is how far.
Distance = the S-minus-P interval × 8 km per second, because the two waves left together and travel at different speeds.
The S minus P interval is 13 seconds
Distance is about 8 km for each second of that gap
Why the number moved
Explain 6.6 against 6.8
Hazard & Forecasting
Tanaka has both agency bulletins on the desk. The early one used the first stations to report; the later one used the whole network and the long-period part of the record.
An early magnitude is a first estimate on partial data, and a revision is the method working rather than failing.
a magnitude is computed from records, so more records can change it
What does the change from 6.6 to 6.8 tell the public?

An automatic magnitude is computed in minutes from whichever stations have reported, using the part of the record that arrives first. A large earthquake keeps radiating energy at long periods for tens of seconds after that, and only the full network and the long-period part of the signal capture all of it. So early estimates of big events run low and get revised up. Nothing about the ground changed between the two bulletins; the measurement got better.
The earthquake grew stronger during the six hours between the two bulletins.
The later figure used more stations and the long-period signal.
One of the two agencies made an error that should be corrected publicly.
The two figures are on different scales and cannot be compared at all.
The earthquake was over in under a minute; nothing about it changed six hours later.
Neither agency was wrong — each stated what its data supported at the time it was issued.
Both figures are moment magnitudes on the same scale, which is why they can be compared at all.
A notice somebody acts on
Say it in a way that survives being repeated
Public Safety
Adeyemi has two hundred words and an audience that has heard two numbers and a rumour about a bigger one coming. She wants to know what the notice has to contain.
A notice earns its place by changing what somebody does, and everything else in it competes with that.
a public notice is read once, quickly, by somebody who is tired

People act on the first thing they can use, so the action goes first: what to do about the building you are standing outside. The reason comes next, because a reason is what makes an instruction survive being repeated by somebody else. The magnitude revision belongs third — it matters, but nobody does anything differently because of it — and the aftershock forecast last, framed as a rate, because it is the part most likely to be misread as a prediction of a particular event.
What to do about the building you are standing outside.
Why, in one sentence.
That the magnitude was revised from 6.6 to 6.8, and what that does and does not mean.
The aftershock forecast, stated as a rate per week.
What the placard is claiming
Learn what a rapid assessment can honestly say, and what it cannot.
Four hundred buildings were placarded in two days by six people. Somebody has to say what that is worth.

Sunday, and the first placards are being argued about. Alan Whitcombe's team got through four hundred buildings in two days, which is fast, and Whitcombe is the first to say what that speed bought and what it cost. A green placard on a house in the Flats means an engineer stood outside it for six minutes. Yvette Delacroix has residents asking whether green means safe, and Peter Ives at the hospital wants to know why his yellow has not moved in three days. Today you work out what a rapid assessment actually inspects, what a placard colour is claiming, and which buildings have to be looked at again properly.
A placard states what an inspection covered, and the ones that go wrong are the ones read as covering more.
Six minutes outside a building
Say what a rapid assessment actually samples
Structural Assessment
Whitcombe's form has eleven boxes and a place for the colour. He filled four hundred of them in two days, and he has kept a second list of everything he did not look at.
A rapid assessment samples the outside and the obvious, so a green placard is a statement about what was visible.
an inspection covers what the inspector could see

A rapid assessment is a triage tool. It is meant to clear the obviously safe and stop the obviously dangerous being entered, quickly, when there are more buildings than engineers. What it can see is exterior damage, gross leaning, and the condition of the visible load path. What it cannot see is anything behind a lining, any connection inside a wall, the state of a foundation, or damage in a part of the building nobody opened. The colour is honest about none of that unless the form is read with it, which is why the second list matters more than the first.
Covered — this is what a walk-past is for.
Not covered, and no colour on the door implies anything about it.
Not covered without survey or excavation.
Not covered, and the form should record that nobody got in.
Cracking visible from the street is exactly what a rapid assessment is designed to catch.
A connection inside a wall cannot be seen from outside and is not covered by the walk-past.
Foundation condition needs excavation or survey, neither of which happens in six minutes.
Damage in an unopened part of a building is invisible to any exterior inspection.
Cracking in the visible outside walls.
A steel connection buried inside a wall lining.
The state of the foundation under the building.
The rear wing, which was locked and nobody entered.
Green does not mean safe
Explain what green means to somebody standing in the street
Public Safety
Delacroix has three residents outside with green placards and one question between them: is my house all right? Adeyemi will not say yes and needs a sentence that is not a dodge.
A verdict covers what was looked at, and its wording should not promise more.
people read a colour as a verdict
What does a green placard entitle somebody to be told?

The honest sentence is narrow and it is still useful: an engineer looked, from outside and from what was accessible, and found nothing that stops you going in. It says nothing about the parts nobody could see, nothing about repairs, and nothing about the next earthquake. Saying more than that is how a green placard becomes a promise, and a promise is what gets broken when an aftershock finds the connection nobody opened a wall to look at.
That the building is safe to live in and has been checked throughout.
That no restriction was found from what could be inspected, and what was not inspected is listed.
That the building came through undamaged and needs no repair work.
That the building will withstand any aftershock in the forecast.
Nothing in a rapid assessment checks a whole building, so "checked throughout" is untrue.
Green is not a statement about repair work; plenty of green buildings need it.
No placard is a claim about future shaking, and the forecast is a rate rather than a guarantee.
The ones worth a second visit
Decide which buildings get looked at again
Hazard & Forecasting
Two engineers are free tomorrow. Tanaka lays out four candidates from the four hundred, each of which somebody has asked about.
Re-inspect where the first look was least able to see and the consequence of being wrong is largest.
a second inspection is a scarce thing to spend
Which building gets the detailed evaluation first?

Two things decide this: how much the first inspection could not see, and what it costs to be wrong. The hospital is worst on both. It has ninety people inside it now, it is holding a yellow that nobody can resolve without opening the plant room, and every day it stays yellow is a day the district's care is running somewhere else. The red warehouse is empty and already restricted, so nothing changes today. The two green buildings are low consequence, and anxiety, while real, is a reason for a phone call rather than for an engineer.
The hospital, yellow, occupied by ninety patients, with an unopened plant room.
A green two-storey shop with a cracked front step.
A red warehouse, empty, on the port, with an obvious lean.
A green house whose owner is anxious and has called four times.
A cracked front step is a non-structural defect on a low-consequence building.
The warehouse is empty and red; a second look changes nothing about who is at risk today.
An anxious owner deserves an explanation, which is a different resource from an engineer's day.
The building that looks worst
Separate what frightens people from what is actually holding the building up.
Marina Court is leaning eight degrees and its structure is undamaged. The queue outside it is not about engineering.

Monday, and Marina Court is on the front page. Six storeys of flats sitting over at eight degrees above the marina, photographed from the water, and the photograph has done more to frighten this town than anything the office has said. Elena Navarro has been under it: the raft foundation is uncracked, the frame is plumb within itself, and the columns show nothing. Bram Halvorsen wants it demolished this week because of what it is doing to people. Marisol Okonkwo will not sign a demolition of a sound building on the strength of a photograph, and today she is right. Today you work out what actually failed, what the lean costs, and what a demolition would and would not fix.
A building can fail without breaking, and the thing that failed may be the ground it stands on.
The raft is fine and the building is not
Which explanation fits every observation?
Geotechnical
Navarro's survey: the raft is intact, level within itself, and rotated. One side has gone down 340 millimetres and the other has come up 90. The sand fans are worst on the low side.
A structure can fail without anything in the structure breaking.
a foundation spreads a building's weight into the ground
A six-storey block is eight degrees out of plumb, with no damage to its structure.

Everything points down rather than up. The frame is plumb within itself and the raft is uncracked, so nothing in the building yielded — a structural failure cannot produce a perfect rotation of an undamaged box. Settlement on one edge with heave on the other is exactly what happens when soil under one side turns to a heavy liquid and squeezes out sideways, and the ejecta in the street on the low side is that soil arriving at the surface. The building did what it was built to do; the ground stopped doing what everyone assumed it would.
The frame failed and the lean is structural
A frame that has yielded on one side would lean this way.
The ground liquefied and lost bearing capacity under one side
Liquefied soil cannot carry the pressure under the raft
The raft was built out of level and this predates the earthquake
A construction fault would produce a permanent lean.
An aftershock struck the building from one side
A directional pulse could push a building over.
A yielded frame shows distortion within itself, and this one is plumb to a tenth of a degree.
A construction fault would have been visible for years and would not come with fresh ejecta.
A single directional pulse does not settle one edge by 340 mm and lift the other.
What eight degrees does
Decide what the lean actually costs
Structural Assessment
Okonkwo has the column loads. At eight degrees the weight above each column no longer lands over its centre, and the offset grows with height up the building.
A lean is dangerous through the extra moment it puts on the frame, not because it looks alarming.
a leaning column carries its load off-centre
What is the engineering objection to leaving Marina Court standing?

A column is very good at being squashed and much worse at being bent. Once the building leans, every floor's weight acts to one side of the column below it, and that offset multiplies up the height into a bending moment nobody designed for. It is a real and computable objection, and it is the one that decides whether people may go back in. Fear is not an engineering reason, and the frame itself has not been damaged — which is exactly why the argument has to be made in moments rather than in adjectives.
That the lean will keep increasing on its own until the building falls over.
That the weight now acts off-centre, adding bending to columns built to be squashed.
That a leaning building is frightening and public confidence matters.
That the frame has been weakened by the rotation itself.
The lean stops when the pore pressure dissipates; it is not a process that runs away by itself.
Public confidence is a real cost and a reason to explain, not a reason a structure is unsafe.
The frame is undamaged, which is precisely what the survey found.
What knocking it down would fix
Answer the demolition question
Public Safety
Halvorsen wants it gone this week. Delacroix points out that the twelve buildings around it stand on the same ground, and nobody is proposing to demolish those.
Demolishing the visible case leaves the condition that produced it, and the condition is under the whole street.
a decision can treat a symptom or a cause

Demolition removes the hazard from this building and none of the hazard from the street. The ground that failed here runs under twelve more blocks, and nothing about knocking down Marina Court tells anybody which of those is next. The measurement that changes decisions is a ground investigation across the Flats, because it is the only one that generalises. Straightening the building is real engineering and slow. Doing nothing is not available — the lean has to be monitored — but monitoring is cheap and buys the time the investigation needs.
Investigate the ground across the Flats
Monitor the lean weekly and leave the cordon in place while that runs.
Demolish Marina Court this week and reassure the town.
Underpin and straighten the building

The raft is uncracked and the frame is plumb within itself. Twelve blocks stand on the same
fill. Demolition would take three weeks and cost about the same as investigating the whole
Flats. Nobody is inside the building. The lean has not changed in three days of readings.
The one everybody assumed was fine
Look at a green building properly, and find what a walk-past could never see.
Bay Road School is green, term starts in a week, and nobody has been inside the gym.

Tuesday, and the school is the quiet problem. Bay Road School came through with a green placard, its classrooms look untouched, and the district would like four hundred children back in it next week. Alan Whitcombe placarded it on day one from outside and wrote on his second list that the gymnasium was locked. The gym is a single-storey hall with a long-span roof, no internal walls, and heavy precast panels for its side walls. Marisol Okonkwo has the keys this morning. Today you work out what a long-span hall does in an earthquake, what holds its walls to its roof, and whether four hundred children go into it on Monday.
The dangerous building is often the one nobody looked at, because nothing about it invited a second look.
A hall with nothing in the middle
Find where the load path stops
Structural Assessment
The gym is 34 metres across with a steel truss roof and precast concrete side panels. The classrooms next door are small rooms with walls every four metres and no damage at all.
A wall is only as good as its connection to the roof, and a long-span hall has few places to make that connection.
a horizontal force has to travel through a building to reach the ground

In the classroom block the earthquake force meets a wall every four metres and goes straight down: short paths, plenty of them, nothing to break. The gym has none of that. Its force has to travel along the roof to the end walls, which means the roof has to act as a stiff plate and the panels have to be tied to it well enough to drag along. Every one of those requirements is a connection, and connections are what fail. The panels themselves are strong and they are the last thing to worry about.
Carries the force straight down over a short path, many times over.
Has to act as a stiff plate and carry the force sideways to the end walls.
Has to drag the wall along with the roof, and is the smallest thing in the chain.
Is strong in its own plane, and was never the weak part.
Walls every four metres give the classroom block a short, redundant path to the ground.
